q-125482.name: Question 1
q-125482.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise.
q-125482.worked_solution:
The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$

q-125482.html:
Question 1
?

Calculate the circulation Γ of the vector field F(x,y)=1yi+1xj along the circle C with equation x2+y2=9 oriented counterclockwise.

a
9π
b
−3π
c
0
d
−9π
e
3π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The closed curve C is the circle of radius 3 centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as r(t)=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,0≤t≤2π.

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

So,

F(r(t))=1yi+1xj=13sin⁡ti+13cos⁡tj.

Computing r′(t), we get

r′(t)=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj.

Therefore,

F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(13sin⁡ti+13cos⁡tj)⋅(−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj)=13sin⁡t⋅(−3sin⁡t)+13cos⁡t⋅3cos⁡t=−1+1=0.

Hence, we conclude that:

Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫02πF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=0

q-125640.name: Question 2
q-125640.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152067/assets/a1883ee3a3a99d43109bae2d2093aef35548dde9753cfb7dc19dfd77a104ec83.png)

Consider the ellipse $E$ and the vector field $F,$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $E$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

II. ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

III. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$
q-125640.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement III is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves counterclockwise along $C.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152067/assets/8595904122fac3431fc959b2fa4aa5a3062bd1bffd1a391a0861fa12f2498054.png)

So, ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

- Statement II is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves **clockwise** along $C.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14152067/assets/f1f31f2b6eefddedc46b8e845703904c0b4566963e64a644f7a4ab32bb7240c3.png)

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

I. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$

II. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

III. ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion.

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
